caption:
Did Mary Toft really give birth to rabbits? No. She confessed on 7 December 1726.

Toft was a 24-year-old field worker from Godalming, Surrey. In 1726 she became pregnant and miscarried. Soon after, she began producing animal parts, and local man-midwife John Howard delivered what he described as rabbits — one letter claimed a twelfth rabbit was "now leaping" inside her.

The court took notice. King George I sent Nathaniel St André, surgeon to the Royal Household, who examined her and concluded the rabbits were bred in her fallopian tubes. He published a 40-page pamphlet defending the case on 3 December. Four days later she confessed.

Surgeon Cyriacus Ahlers had already spotted cut marks made by a man-made instrument, plus straw and grain in the droppings. A porter at the bagnio admitted he had been bribed to smuggle a rabbit into her chamber. Toft admitted animal parts had been inserted into her body — cat claws, a rabbit's head.

She was jailed as a "vile cheat and impostor", then discharged on 8 April 1727 without charge because nobody could decide what to charge her with. Howard was fined £800. St André's career never recovered.

Still unresolved: who devised it. Her unpublished confessions blamed her mother-in-law, Howard, and a travelling woman who told her the scheme would mean she'd "never want as long as I liv'd". Her sister-in-law Margaret refused to say anything at all.

Images: portrait of Toft by John Laguerre, 1726; Hogarth's Cunicularii, 1726; the Doctors in Labour broadsheet, 1726; John Clark's etching of Doctor Meagre, c.1726; James Caulfield's engraving, 1819; Hogarth's Credulity, Superstition and Fanaticism, 1762. All public domain.

cards.headline: In 1726 she convinced the <y>king's surgeon</y> she was birthing rabbits
cards.note: Mary Toft of Godalming, Surrey. Painted while she sat in prison.
cards.source: Portrait of Mary Toft by John Laguerre, 1726
cards.alt: Painted portrait of a seated woman in a lace cap holding a white rabbit in her lap.

cards.headline: She said a rabbit <y>startled her in a field</y>
cards.note: Working while pregnant, she chased one and lost it. Then she miscarried, and said she could think of nothing else.
cards.alt: Printed satirical broadsheet with rows of small engraved scenes and verse beneath each.

cards.headline: A surgeon wrote that the <y>twelfth rabbit was 'now leaping'</y>
cards.note: John Howard invited anyone who doubted him to come and watch a delivery. Henry Davenant of the royal court came, and believed.
cards.source: Hogarth, 'Cunicularii, or The Wise Men of Godliman', 1726
cards.alt: Etching of a woman in labour on a bed surrounded by wigged men, rabbits on the floor.

cards.headline: The royal surgeon concluded rabbits <y>bred in her fallopian tubes</y>
cards.note: Nathaniel St André tested a rabbit lung in water to see if it had breathed. He staked his reputation on a 40-page pamphlet.
cards.source: Engraving of Mary Toft by James Caulfield, 1819
cards.alt: Stipple engraving of a seated woman in a lace cap, a small rabbit on her lap.

cards.headline: Cut marks, <y>straw and grain in the droppings</y>
cards.note: Surgeon Cyriacus Ahlers took specimens home. He found they had been cut with a man-made instrument.
cards.alt: Etching of a French surgeon bowing with a letter before a tall thin doctor in an interior.

cards.headline: She confessed: <y>the parts were inserted</y> into her body
cards.note: Discharged in 1727 — nobody knew what to charge her with. Who devised the plot was never settled.
cards.alt: Detail of a Hogarth engraving: a woman lying on the floor with small rabbits beside her.
